newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to slow down high-speed trains plans.
newsitem.headline: France to slow down high-speed trains plans.

text.p: France said on Tuesday financial constraints would force it to slow down plans to extend its costly 300-kmph (190-mph) high-speed TGV rail network.

Junior transport minister Anne-Marie Idrac said lower than expected profitability of TGV trains and widespread austerity as France struggles to cut its budget deficit to meet crieria for the European Union single currency in 1999 had forced a review of the plans.
"The TGV programme must continue but progress must be compatible with the financial resources that the nation can afford," Idrac told a seminar.

She said it would take a generation to complete plans to add 2,300 km (1,440 miles) of proposed high-speed lines to the existing 1,300 km (820 miles) connecting Paris with Valence in the south, Rennes in the West, Bordeaux in the southwest and Lille in the North.
Building the extensions would cost more than 200 billion francs ($40 billion), not including the cost of trains, she said.
Idrac said a 24-billion-franc ($4.8-billion) extension of the southern line to the Mediterranean port of Marseille, already under way, would be completed by 2000 as planned.

The next route to be built will connect Paris to Strasbourg on the German border. But it will be constructed in stages and will be the first to be equipped with pendular TGV trains -- trains that can reach high speeds on cheaper conventional lines.

Idrac gave no date for the completion of the line to Strasbourg and made no mention of other proposed high-speed routes to the Spanish border and the Italian city of Turin through a tunnel under the Alps.
She said 10 percent of the line to Strasbourg could be financed by the European Union and added: "The problem of the eastern TGV is...the remaining 90 percent".

The government is studying alternative ways of financing TGV lines, increasing the share of local authorities, in order to cut the snowballing deficit of the heavily-indebted state-run SNCF railway company.

Idrac said the government would pay special attention to pendular trains, a technology which has been ignored in France so far but would allow the opening of high-speed routes without equipping them with special track.
TGV manufacturers GEC-Alsthom would deliver the first pendular prototype next year and start producing pendular trains in 2000.

Idrac dismissed criticism that pendular TGVs were the poor man's TGVs. She said they would be able to travel at TGV speeds of 300-350 kmh (190-220 mph) on TGV lines and 220 kmh (140 mph) on conventional track.
